exclusions.A: Maria told her not to touch 'em, for fear of getting her feet wet and cutting her fingers.
exclusions.B: My sister Bessie don't try half so hard to help people.
exclusions.C: She only plays while there's work going on; and only see how much work I've done this morning!
exclusions.D: She thinks Susan is the best of all our dolls, but I don't.

PD2-P1-6.note: The narrator looks down on Bessie for tending her doll and playing while (as the narrator sees it) work goes on: 'Bessie isn't so much use as I am.' The worry about cut fingers is Maria's, and the needle-watching comes only in the fifth paragraph.

exclusions.A: The visitor walks along dark alleys lined on both sides with these brilliant tanks, and the beautiful sea animals are so close that it seems easy to touch them.
exclusions.B: There are about thirty tanks in all, and at the very first of these glass-walled vats we stopped entranced.
exclusions.D: The light comes only from above, shining through water of many hundreds of cubic feet, on to what seems at first a garden of moving flowers behind tanks of clear glass, which seem, so complete is the illusion, not like glass at all, but water.
exclusions.E: It is like being in a narrow, dark theater with the stage all around and about, strangely illuminated, not by footlights, but by a radiance from above.

PD2-P5-2.note: The writer admires the overhead lighting for the complete illusion it creates (the glass seems like water, a stage lit by radiance from above); touching only 'seems' easy and comes from closeness, and the dark alleys are described with delight, not unease.

exclusions.A: When one reads that he heard the bookworm crow like a cock, and said, "I knew not whether some local fowl was clamoring or whether there was but a beating in my ears," one can not help wondering if there was not something defective in his ear drums; but further on he says, "I perceived, in the paper whereon I was writing, a little insect that ceased not to carol like very chanticleer, until taking a magnifying glass I assiduously observed him."
exclusions.B: From this one concludes that if the fault were not with his hearing, by which some well-known sounds made by book insects seemed to him like the crowing of a cock, an altogether different cock from the kind we know must have lived in his day.
exclusions.C: A curious and interesting characterization of some species of book insects has come to us in the writings of Christian Mentzel, the German naturalist and philologist, who lived in the seventeenth century.
exclusions.D: Reaction against these weird and fantastical accounts is indicated by the question, not infrequently asked, "Are there such things as bookworms?"

PD2-P4-5.note: The author treats Mentzel's crowing-cock comparison with wry humor (his ear drums, or a different kind of cock in his day), not respect, suspicion of fabrication, indignation or real worry. A (respect for his care) is the strongest distractor but is undercut by the joking tone.

exclusions.A: When we talk about climate change “reshaping” our world, we often mean it’s reshaping our attitudes, actions, and politics.
exclusions.B: And without the science, we cannot hope to address or adapt to climate change’s impacts on them.
exclusions.C: But at Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah, the effects of climate change may be literally reshaping the physical park.
exclusions.E: Warmer temperatures resulting from climate change could pose a grave threat to the park’s iconic natural rock structures, the hoodoos, whose creation apparently rely on cycles of freezing and thawing water.

PD2-P6-5.note: The author worries that warming 'could pose a grave threat' to the hoodoos; the harm is prospective (so not mournful over loss), no adaptation plans exist without the science, and the mention of attitudes and politics is neutral, neither approving nor scornful.
